Chapter 4: The Impact of Mass Incarceration and Police Violence
The shadow of the criminal justice system wasn’t just a distant threat—it hung over the community like a storm cloud. For so many families, the fear of losing someone they loved to incarceration was always present. And the reasons? Sometimes it was something as small as missing a court date, getting caught up in a minor infraction, or even just being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
But the consequences? They were life-changing. Families found themselves torn apart. Kids grew up without their parents. And dreams—dreams that once felt so within reach—were suddenly derailed by a system that seemed built more for punishment than for helping people get back on track.
I want you to imagine a family where one brother’s struggles with mental health made him especially vulnerable. Every time he crossed paths with the police, things seemed to escalate. Instead of care and compassion, he was met with suspicion—and sometimes force. His family fought so hard for him, trying to cut through layers of bureaucracy that felt cold and unfeeling. Every setback was a harsh reminder of how little value the system placed on Black lives, especially for those dealing with mental illness.
And it wasn’t just about the person who was locked up. The impact of incarceration rippled out, touching everyone around them. Families had to carry the weight of stigma and the heavy financial burden that comes with supporting a loved one behind bars. Visiting jails, sitting in courtrooms—these became regular, painful routines. The toll it took, emotionally and financially, was huge. But so was the determination to keep pushing back, to keep fighting for something better.
Stories about police violence? Unfortunately, they were everywhere. Friends and neighbors would talk about encounters with the police that ended with someone getting hurt, or humiliated. Just the thought of being stopped by the police was enough to change the way people went about their daily lives. Simple things—walking to the corner store, driving to work—suddenly carried a real sense of danger.
Over time, it became clear that these weren’t just random events. They were part of a bigger pattern—a system that wasn’t neutral at all. The criminal justice system, instead of treating everyone fairly, played a big role in keeping inequality alive. Whenever people talked about “law and order,” it often seemed like code for targeting Black communities, painting them as if they were somehow more dangerous or criminal.
But here’s what’s incredible: the community didn’t let itself be silenced. If anything, the struggle fueled even more organizing and activism. Families and local leaders came together, demanding real change and holding people accountable. Protests, petitions, town halls—they became powerful ways to raise awareness and build a sense of unity. The fight for justice was exhausting, sure, but it was also empowering. It showed that when people come together, they really can make a difference.
And through all of this, something else became clear—healing matters. The trauma left by this system runs deep, and overcoming it takes more than just changing a few laws. It means supporting each other, creating spaces where people can process their pain and start to hope again. Because in the end, that hope and community are what keep the fight alive.
